19 A racing car has an output power of 300 kW when travelling at a constant speed of 60 m s–1.
What is the total resistive force acting on the car?
A
5 kN
B
10 kN
C
50 kN
D
100 kN

hints: Notice the car moves at constant speed of $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so the forward driving force must exactly balance the total backward resistive force.
Connect output power of $300 \text{ kW}$ to force and velocity with $P = Fv$ for motion in the direction of the force.
Convert $300 \text{ kW}$ to $300000 \text{ W}$ and divide by $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ to find $F$ in newtons, then express in $\text{kN}$.
walkthrough: At constant velocity the resultant force is zero, so the driving force $F$ from the engine equals the total resistive force opposing the $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ motion.
Useful power for a force moving its point of application is $P = Fv$, where $P$ is in watts, $F$ in newtons and $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
Substitute $P = 300 \text{ kW} = 300000 \text{ W}$ and $v = 60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$: $F = 300000 / 60 = 5000 \text{ N}$.
Convert to kilonewtons: $5000 \text{ N} = 5.0 \text{ kN}$, which balances the resistive force. This is option A.

A.explanation: At $5000 \text{ N}$ the resistive force equals the driving force, giving $P = Fv = 5.0 \text{ kN}$ times $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: Doubling the correct force to $10 \text{ kN}$ would give $600 \text{ kW}$ at $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, twice the given output power.

C.explanation: A force of $50 \text{ kN}$ would need $3000 \text{ kW}$ at $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, ten times too large, from a power-of-ten error.

D.explanation: A force of $100 \text{ kN}$ would need $6000 \text{ kW}$ at $60 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, twenty times too large.
